It''s design. HDFC, founded in 1994, seized this opportunity by targeting urban professionals and businesses—the most profitable segment."],["p",{},"The structural problem: India''s financial system is bifurcated. A farmer with land cannot access loans because land is illiquid collateral in HDFC''s risk models. A street vendor with zero credit history is invisible."],["li",{},["strong",{},"Remittance monopolies"],": HDFC charges 1.5-3% on domestic money transfers—invisible taxes on workers sending wages home. India Post charges 0.5%, but lacks technology and reach."],["li",{},["strong",{},"Debt trap machinery"],": HDFC''s credit card products and personal loans target middle-class aspirants, creating debt cycles that benefit the bank, not the borrower. Monthly interest rates of 2.5-3% (30-36% annualized) are legal, normalized, and profitable."],["li",{},["strong",{},"Digital gatekeeping"],": HDFC''s app requires smartphone, internet, and biometric authentication. 400 million Indians lack reliable digital access, automatically excluded."]],["h2",{"id":"the-india-post-alternative-that-wasnt"},"The ",["mark",{},"India Post"]," Alternative That Wasn''t"],["p",{},"Here''s the counterfactual: ",["mark",{},"India Post"]," reaches 650,000 pin codes—more than any bank. A postal savings account earns 4% interest, while HDFC deposits earn negative real returns (inflation minus interest). Why? Because Post Office doesn''t charge fees. It doesn''t extract wealth. It''s infrastructure, not profit."],["p",{},"The result: wealthy Indians use HDFC for convenience, access, and financial products. Poor Indians use Post Office because they have no choice.
